subtype: Approach: learning from a rejection debrief [Revision]
passage: I sit behind Mehak in the lab, so I saw how it went. The week her technical round went badly at the first company, she came in with red eyes and said very little. She opened a notebook and wrote down each question she had missed: what a deadlock is, the difference between a process and a thread, why a column gets an index. Then she spent our free lab hours reading about those exact things, instead of skipping them. Two weeks later she came out of the second company's test and said, "They asked about deadlock, and I knew it." I cannot say whether she was scared or fine. I only saw the notebook, and her shoulders drop. — Yash

qa.q: What did Mehak write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote down each question she had missed, such as the difference between a process and a thread.

qa.q: What might Mehak have felt after the technical round, judging by what Yash saw?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and low, since she came in with red eyes and said very little, though Yash admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Mehak use for the next company, and why?
qa.a: She could do a mock technical round with a classmate, because the notebook fixes concepts but a live round tests explaining them aloud.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash to watch Mehak without knowing what she feels?
qa.a: Yash can only guess from the notebook and her dropping shoulders, so Yash stays careful about claiming she was scared or fine.

grounding: Shows a classmate's account of someone writing down missed technical questions, learning the concepts, and finding the next company's questions easier.

subtype: Approach: learning from a rejection debrief [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday. Ishita walked out of the technical round knowing it was over. That night, still stinging, she opened a notebook and wrote down every question she remembered missing: "reverse a linked list in place," "difference between a process and a thread," "why is this query slow?"
The following Sunday. Ishita had spent every evening on those three topics, two evenings each, working through the concepts and a few related problems. On a video call, her senior Jagdish quizzed her. She explained threads with a kitchen analogy and laughed. "I actually get it now."
Three weeks later. In a different company's technical round, the interviewer asked about a slow database query. Ishita recognised the shape of it at once. She talked through the missing index calmly and even sketched a small table. Walking out, she texted Jagdish: "Same kind of question. Felt easy this time."

qa.q: Which questions did Ishita write down?
qa.a: Reverse a linked list in place, difference between a process and a thread, and why is this query slow.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling the night after the rejection?
qa.a: Ishita was still stinging and disappointed, yet determined enough to list every missed question.

qa.q: What else could Ishita add to the debrief next time?
qa.a: Ishita could also note what went well and ask the recruiter for feedback, so the list covers more than memory.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see Ishita's progress?
qa.a: Jagdish, who quizzed her, sees the concepts click and later gets her text, likely feeling proud of how she turned the rejection into learning.

grounding: Shows a student who failed a technical round writing down every missed question, learning the concepts, and finding the next company's questions easier.

subtype: Approach: learning from a rejection debrief [Revision]
passage: Baljeet, you've been sulking since that interview. Sit. Let me tell you about my first rejection, twenty-two years ago. I was twenty-one, top of my class, and I failed the technical round of the first company that came to our campus. The interviewer asked what a hash collision was. I gave a textbook line and then went blank. On the bus back, my friend Sudha said, "Rukmini, crying won't help. Write it down." So that night I wrote every question I'd missed. Hashing, one sorting question, one about recursion. I spent two weeks on just those, from the basics. The next company asked me to design a small phone directory. I used hashing, explained collisions, and got the offer. That notebook of missed questions taught me more than any class. Your rejection has questions in it too, Baljeet.

qa.q: What did the interviewer ask Rukmini?
How did Rukmini feel after failing the technical round?
qa.a: Rukmini was upset and close to tears on the bus, after going blank despite being top of the class.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the difference?
qa.a: The choice that night to write down every missed question and spend two weeks learning those concepts from the basics.

qa.q: How did Sudha respond on the bus?
qa.a: Sudha saw Rukmini's distress and gave a practical push, saying to write it down rather than cry over it.

grounding: Illustrates a student who, after failing a technical round, writes down each missed question, learns the concepts and does better at the next company.
